questions.q: An object of height 3 cm is placed 18 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm, forming an image on a white screen. Find the distance of the image from the mirror, in centimetres. Give the magnitude.
questions.solution:
Use the New Cartesian Sign Convention throughout: distances are measured from the pole, and those on the same side as the incoming light are negative.

**Given.** $u = -18$ cm, $f = -12$ cm (a concave mirror has a negative focal length), $h = +3$ cm.

**Step 1 — the mirror formula.**

$$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u}.$$

**Step 2 — substitute.**

$$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-12} - \frac{1}{-18} = -\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{18}.$$

Taking the common denominator 36 :

$$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{-3 + 2}{36} = -\frac{1}{36} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = -36\ \text{cm}.$$

The image is **36 cm** in front of the mirror. The negative sign says it is on the same side as the object, which is exactly what allows it to be caught on a screen — it is **real**.

**The image height, for completeness.**

$$m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-36}{-18} = -2,$$

so $h' = m \times h = -2 \times 3 = -6$ cm. The image is **6 cm tall and inverted**, twice the size of the object.

(Sensible: the object at 18 cm lies between $f = 12$ cm and $2f = 24$ cm, and an object there always gives a real, inverted, magnified image beyond $2f$.)

questions.q: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of:
questions.solution:
The first law of reflection: $\angle i = \angle r$, both measured **from the normal**, not from the surface.

The second law says the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in one plane.

questions.q: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
questions.solution:
A plane mirror gives a **virtual, erect** image of the **same size**, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

It is also **laterally inverted** — your right hand appears as a left hand, which is why an ambulance's lettering is printed backwards.
options: virtual, erect and of the same size

questions.q: A concave mirror forms a virtual, erect and magnified image when the object is placed:
questions.solution:
**Between the pole and the focus** — the only position that gives a concave mirror a virtual image.

This is why a shaving mirror or a dentist's mirror is concave, and why you must hold it close to your face.
options: between the pole and the focus

questions.q: When light passes from air into glass, it bends:
questions.solution:
Glass is optically **denser**, so light slows down and bends **towards the normal**.

Going the other way — glass to air — it speeds up and bends away.

A car driving off tarmac onto sand at an angle swings round for the same reason: one wheel slows before the other.

questions.q: The SI unit of the power of a lens is:
questions.solution:
The **dioptre** (D), which is the reciprocal of the focal length in **metres**.

A converging lens has positive power, a diverging lens negative. Spectacle prescriptions are written in dioptres — $-2.5$ D is a diverging lens for short sight.

questions.q: A concave mirror has a focal length of $12$ cm. Find its radius of curvature, in cm.
questions.solution:
$R = 2f = 2 \times 12 = \mathbf{24}$ cm.

The focus always sits exactly halfway between the pole and the centre of curvature.

questions.q: The speed of light in a medium is $2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. Find its refractive index. (Speed in vacuum $= 3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s.)
questions.solution: $\mu = \dfrac{c}{v} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2 \times 10^{8}} = \mathbf{1.5}$ — which is about the value for ordinary glass.

questions.q: Find the power (in dioptres) of a convex lens of focal length $25$ cm.
questions.solution:
$P = \dfrac{1}{f\text{ in metres}} = \dfrac{1}{0.25} = \mathbf{+4}$ D.

Converting centimetres to metres first is where this calculation is usually lost.

questions.q: An object of height $5$ cm gives an image of height $10$ cm. Find the magnitude of the magnification.
questions.solution: $|m| = \dfrac{h_{i}}{h_{o}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = \mathbf{2}$ — the image is twice the size of the object.

questions.topic: Image formation by a concave mirror
questions.q: Describe the nature, position and size of the image formed by a concave mirror for five positions of the object.
questions.solution:
**1. Object at infinity.** Image **at the focus** — real, inverted, highly diminished (a point). This is how a concave mirror is used to collect sunlight, and how its focal length is measured.

**2. Object beyond C.** Image **between F and C** — real, inverted, diminished.

**3. Object at C.** Image **at C** — real, inverted, **same size**.

**4. Object between C and F.** Image **beyond C** — real, inverted, magnified. (This is a projector's arrangement.)

**5. Object at F.** Image **at infinity** — real, inverted, highly magnified. Used in searchlights and headlamps, where a parallel beam is wanted.

**6. Object between P and F.** Image **behind the mirror** — **virtual**, erect, magnified. The shaving mirror.

**The pattern worth holding on to:** a concave mirror gives a **real** image everywhere except when the object is closer than the focus. Cases 1 and 5 are each other's reverse, and cases 2 and 4 likewise — light paths are reversible.

questions.q: State the laws of refraction, define refractive index, and explain why a pencil in a glass of water looks bent.
questions.solution:
**Laws of refraction.**

1. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in one plane.

2. **Snell's law:** $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \mu$, a constant for the two media.

**Refractive index.** $\mu = \dfrac{\text{speed of light in vacuum}}{\text{speed of light in the medium}}$.

A higher $\mu$ means light travels more slowly in that medium, and bends more on entering it. Water is $1.33$, glass about $1.5$, diamond $2.42$.

**The bent pencil.** Light from the submerged part travels from water into air and bends **away from the normal** at the surface.

Your eye does not know this. It traces the rays back in **straight lines**, so it places the submerged part higher and displaced sideways from where it really is.

The pencil looks broken at the waterline — and the same effect makes a swimming pool look shallower than it is, which is worth remembering before diving in.

questions.q: An object $4$ cm tall is placed $20$ cm from a convex lens of focal length $10$ cm. Find the image position, size and nature, and state the rules for drawing the ray diagram.
questions.solution:
**Using the lens formula** with $u = -20$ cm, $f = +10$ cm:

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{-20} = \dfrac{2 - 1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{20}$

$v = +20$ cm — **positive**, so the image is **real** and on the other side of the lens.

**Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{20}{-20} = -1$.

**Image height:** $-1 \times 4 = -4$ cm — the minus sign means **inverted**.

**Answer:** real, inverted, same size ($4$ cm), $20$ cm on the far side.

An object at $2f$ always gives an image at $2f$, the same size — worth recognising on sight.

**Rules for the ray diagram** (any two are enough):

1. A ray **parallel to the principal axis** passes through the focus after refraction.

2. A ray **through the optical centre** goes straight on, undeviated.

3. A ray **through the focus** emerges parallel to the axis.

Where the two refracted rays meet is the image.

questions.q: State the New Cartesian sign convention for mirrors and lenses, and explain why a negative image distance means a virtual image.
questions.solution:
**The convention.**

1. The **pole** (mirror) or **optical centre** (lens) is the origin.

2. Distances are measured **from** it, along the principal axis.

3. Distances measured in the **same direction as the incident light** are **positive**; against it, **negative**.

4. Heights **above** the axis are positive; **below**, negative.

**Consequences worth memorising:**

• The **object distance $u$ is always negative** (the object is on the incoming side).

• A **concave mirror** has negative $f$; a **convex mirror** positive.

• A **convex lens** has positive $f$; a **concave lens** negative.

**Why negative $v$ means virtual.** For a **mirror**, a real image forms in front, where the light actually goes — the same side as the object, so $v$ is negative there by the convention; behind the mirror, where no light reaches, $v$ is positive and the image is **virtual**.

For a **lens** it is the other way: a real image forms on the far side ($v$ positive), so a negative $v$ puts the image back on the object's side, where the rays only *appear* to come from — virtual.

The sign is not decoration: it is the answer to 'which side is the image on', and hence to whether you could catch it on a screen.

questions.q: Give one use each of a concave mirror, a convex mirror, a convex lens and a concave lens, with the reason.
questions.solution:
**Concave mirror — a car headlamp or a torch.** The bulb is placed at the focus, so the reflected light leaves as a **parallel beam** that travels far without spreading.

Also used as a shaving mirror and by dentists (magnified erect image when held close), and in solar cookers (sunlight concentrated at the focus).

**Convex mirror — a vehicle's rear-view mirror.** It always gives an erect, diminished image and covers a **much wider field of view**, so the driver sees more traffic — at the cost of everything looking further away, which is why such mirrors carry a warning.

Also used as security mirrors at blind corners in shops.

**Convex lens — spectacles for long sight (hypermetropia).** The eye's lens converges too weakly, so the image falls behind the retina; a converging lens gives the extra help.

Also used in a magnifying glass, a camera and a microscope.

**Concave lens — spectacles for short sight (myopia).** The eye converges too strongly and the image falls in front of the retina; a diverging lens pushes it back.

Also used in a peephole in a door and in a Galilean telescope's eyepiece.
